meta.description: Not Poe. The Poe Museum lists "The best things in life make you sweaty" as fake, and Wikiquote traces it to a 2009 web forum comment.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The best things in life make you sweaty'?
meta.ogDescription: Edgar Allan Poe never wrote it. The Poe Museum calls it a fake, and Wikiquote's earliest known source is a 2009 comment on a duck-hunting forum.

answer.label: Not Edgar Allan Poe — an anonymous internet quip
answer.authorDates: Earliest known source per Wikiquote: a 2009 web forum comment
answer.sourceLine: Nobody has found this line anywhere in Poe’s writings. The Poe Museum ↗ lists it as a fake Poe quote, and Wikiquote ↗ files it under “Misattributed.” Wikiquote’s earliest known source is a 2009 comment on a South Carolina duck-hunting website. Who first wrote it is unknown.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

docMeta.dd: No. The line is not traced to any poem, tale, essay or letter
A 2009 comment on a South Carolina duck-hunting website (per Wikiquote)
Museum of Hoaxes (2012) and the Poe Museum (2014)

source.excerpt: The best things in life make you sweaty.
trail: Museum of Hoaxes, June 12, 2012 ↗: “Brief Answer: No!” It says “Poe never said this,” notes that Facebook and Tumblr pages spread the attribution, and says it does not know where the line came from.
Poe Museum, “Did Poe Really Say That?” (Chris Semtner, September 10, 2014) ↗: entry no. 6 says the line “quite obviously is not a Poe statement.”
Wikiquote ↗: listed under “Misattributed.” Its earliest known source is a 2009 comment on a South Carolina duck-hunting website.
source.excerptNote: No longer context exists. The line has never been found in a Poe text, so the excerpt is just the bare quip that circulates online.
source.rightsNote: The line has no identified author and no published source, so we make no claim about its copyright status. It does not come from any of Poe’s works, which are all in the public domain, so his public-domain status does not cover it.

author.name: Edgar Allan Poe
author.kicker: The name it gets pinned on
author.heading: About Edgar Allan Poe
author.bio: Edgar Allan Poe (January 19, 1809 – October 7, 1849) wrote “The Raven,” “The Tell-Tale Heart” and “The Fall of the House of Usher,” and his Dupin stories helped invent detective fiction. Many quotations credited to him online are fakes. The Poe Museum in Richmond, Virginia, keeps a list of them, and this one is on it.

misattribution.heading: How Poe got the credit
misattribution.intro: Quote sites, social-media posts and at least one newspaper column credit this line to Edgar Allan Poe. None of them cites a Poe text.

items.scope: Quote sites, Facebook and Tumblr pages
items.why: The Museum of Hoaxes ↗ found the line credited to Poe on many sites, “facebook and tumblr pages especially.” It concludes that “Poe never said this” and that it was not “the kind of thing he would have said.”

A column by Gordon Mercer and Marcia Gaines Mercer ↗ (posted June 3, 2012) opens with the line, credits it to Poe (1809–1849), and gives Poe “a thumbs up on this quote.” The Museum of Hoaxes noted that the Richmond County Daily Journal ran an article that used the supposed Poe quotation as its lead.

misattribution.truthLine: Poe did not write it. The Poe Museum ↗ lists it among the fake Poe quotes, and Wikiquote ↗ traces its earliest known appearance to a 2009 forum comment by an unknown writer.

context.heading: Why the joke sticks
lead: Much of this line’s appeal comes from the mismatch: a cheerful line about sweat, credited to the gloomiest name in American letters. The Museum of Hoaxes ↗ could not tell whether the people posting it believed Poe said it or were joking. It doubted that sharers knew enough about Poe’s life to get the joke.
Some people clearly did take it straight. A 2012 newspaper column built a whole piece around it as Poe’s advice on hard work. That is how a throwaway line ends up passed around as a real quotation.
context.pull: “Of course, Poe never said this.” — Museum of Hoaxes, 2012
